forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough has £10.6m of in-principle exceptional financial support across 2025/26 and 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council was provided with in-principle capitalisation support of £10.6m across 2025/26 and 2026/27, according to an update to its Audit Committee on the council's Exceptional Financial Support action plan. The support is split £5m in 2025/26 and £5.6m in 2026/27. The council formally requested it from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government in December 2025.

Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The paper says a review by the accountancy body CIPFA assessed financial management, financial sustainability and risk, service reform and transformation, and governance, culture and leadership. It "concluded that the Council had credible plans to improve financial sustainability and reduce its reliance on Exceptional Financial Support." The paper describes this as a conclusion about the plans, not a statement that they have been delivered.

The action plan appendix rates one recommendation, number 8 on reserves, as High, scoring it 9. It states: "Reserves remain low and mean that the council does not have the financial resilience to deal with unexpected financial shocks, remaining reliant on Exceptional Financial Support." The action listed is to set a risk-based minimum reserves level as a percentage of net revenue expenditure, and to monitor replenishment against the medium-term financial strategy.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough has government approval to capitalise £9.7m of costs; SEND report raises further support
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council has agreed with government to capitalise £9.7m of extraordinary day-to-day spending pressures under exceptional financial support, permission from government to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The medium-term financial strategy before Cabinet on 27 October 2026 says the sum is made up of £4.0m for 2025/26 and £5.7m for 2026/27.

The approval followed a review by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA), published on 18 August. The strategy says the review found significant improvements in financial management and governance, and that challenges remain, including rebuilding reserves and pressures in children's social care.

A separate Cabinet report on reform of support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) says the council would need to consider exceptional financial support again. It links this to the council's low reserve balances and to the possibility that the Department for Education funds only 90% of future deficits. The report says "the Council would need to consider Exceptional Financial Support to fund this", meaning the remaining 10%.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough forecasts £7.9m overspend on £258m budget, £7.7m of it in children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to spend £7.9m more than planned in 2026/27 on its day-to-day running costs (revenue spending: staff, services and contracts). That is 3.1% over a net budget of £258m, according to a first-quarter report to its cabinet on 1 October. Children and Young People accounts for £7.7m of the total.

The largest single line is placements for children in care, forecast to overspend by £5.2m. The budget assumed 429 children in care and 41 residential placements. The number of children in care was 444 in June, and residential placements stood at 47 in August. The average price of the last ten residential placements is £9,000 a week against £6,500 budgeted, and nine children are in placements costing more than £10,000 a week. Residential care makes up £3.2m of the £5.2m placement overspend.

If the overspend continues to the year end, the council will have to draw on its general fund reserves, the money set aside as a cushion for the unexpected. The report forecasts the balance falling from £10.5m at the start of the year to £6.7m by 31 March 2027, a 36% reduction. Total usable reserves, money the council can actually spend, are £23.7m, excluding the deficit on schools funding. Of that, £6.8m, or 29%, is ringfenced for specific purposes.

findings.headline: Training for Audit Committee members is ongoing, with 3/7 members having completed the mandatory training
findings.detail: Recommendation 2 notes that training for members of the Audit Committee is ongoing, with Statement of Accounts and Treasury Management sessions held in June and September. The paper says only 2/5 reserve members have completed the mandatory training.
findings.matters: The paper ties the completion rate to whether challenge from the committee can be assessed, which bears on the quality of scrutiny in other councils' audit committees as well.
findings.quote: Only 3/7 Audit Committee members have completed the mandatory training.

findings.headline: Two Senior Auditors were appointed to Internal Audit and commenced at the start of September 2026.
findings.detail: Recommendation 1 is marked COMPLETED. The paper says a further post is being filled with temporary resources, and that Internal Audit still relies on external capacity from RSM to deliver the audit plan.
findings.matters: Internal audit capacity affects the ability to deliver the audit plan and assess internal controls, which finance directors and lenders watch when judging governance.
findings.quote: Two Senior Auditors were appointed and commenced within Internal Audit at the start of September 2026.

findings.headline: The 2025/26 audit is in flight, with the Audit Report expected in December.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has not had a full audit for several years. It reports weekly meetings between the S151 Officer and EY, early feedback recognising improved responsiveness and quality of working papers, and a December 2026 review point.
findings.matters: A council with no full audit for several years is watched closely by lenders and peers for the first clean or qualified opinion in that period.
findings.quote: 2025/26 audit is in flight and Audit Report expected in December.

findings.headline: An ICB offer letter dated 28.09.2026 to resolve outstanding debt is recorded in the health funding dispute.
findings.detail: Recommendation 12 concerns the dispute with health statutory partners, which the council may have to fund in full, with potential effects on EFS and on its ability to contribute to reserves. The action owner reports significant progress and active negotiation.
findings.matters: Unresolved health contributions can increase the EFS requirement, so a finance officer or lender will track whether the dispute is being settled.
findings.quote: Offer letter received from ICB 28.09.2026 to resolve debt outstanding.

findings.headline: The paper states that the financial consequences of increased placement costs, churn and numbers in Children's Services are "substantial", causing "a significant in year pressure".
findings.detail: The action owner records this in relation to the Children's Social Care position. Recommendation 17 includes a multi-year demand and placement forecasting model, and recommendation 18 creates a high-cost placement panel.
findings.matters: Placement cost growth is a common source of council overspend, and a peer finance officer can compare the forecasting and panel approach against their own.
findings.quote: the financial consequences of the increases in placement costs, churn and increased numbers are substantial causing a significant in year pressure.

daily_post.headline: The council is the subject of a paused Local Government Reorganisation and will remain responsible for local services for at least one additional MTFS year.
daily_post.lead: A finance director elsewhere in a two-tier or reorganising area would want to know how the pause changes the timetable for stable baselines and transition funding.
